# Pāsādika Sutta (DN 29 (PTS DN iii 117))

**ID:** DN 29 (PTS DN iii 117)
**Section:** Dīghanikāya (dn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Pāsādika Sutta
**PTS:** DN iii 117
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0103m.mul5.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Pāsādika Sutta* (DN 29) is a major discourse delivered by the Buddha while dwelling among the Sakyans, prompted by the recent death of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta at Pāvā and the ensuing sectarian fragmentation and quarreling among his Jain followers [Gethin 2001; Norman 1983]. When the novice Cunda reports these schismatic events to Ānanda, both approach the Buddha, who addresses Cunda on the contrast between an ill-proclaimed doctrine and a well-expounded dispensation [Gethin 2001; Freedman 1977]. The Buddha explains that the completeness of his holy life is reflected in the spiritual accomplishment of the fourfold assembly, notably requiring the order of nuns [Anālayo 2016]. He also addresses the nature of the Tathāgata's knowledge of the past and future [Pandey 1972]. To preserve the Dhamma and avoid future discord after his passing, the Buddha exhorts the community to recite the teachings in harmony, comparing meaning to meaning and phrasing to phrasing, specifically centering on the factors leading to awakening [Peoples 2013; Gethin 2001]. The discourse concludes with the elder Upavāna fanning the Buddha [Freedman 1977].

- Resembling parallels: AN 9.7 Sutavāsutta; AN 9.8 Sajjhasutta; MN 76 (PTS MN i 513) Sandaka Sutta; SF 58

**Sources**

- [Gethin 2001] R. M. Gethin, The Buddhist Path to Awakening: A Study of the Bodhi-Pakkhiyā Dhammā (2001 [1992]) — Setting after Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta's death, Cunda and Ānanda's involvement, the call for recitation of Dhamma, and comparison with the Sāmagāma Sutta.
- [Norman 1983] K. R. Norman, Pāli Literature (1983) — Notes the common historical context of Jain feuding after Nātaputta's death shared by DN 29 and DN 33.
- [Freedman 1977] Michael Freedman, The Characterization of Ānanda in the Pāli Canon of the Theravāda (1977) — Details on Cunda, Ānanda, the Buddha addressing Cunda, and Upavāna fanning the Buddha at the close.
- [Anālayo 2016] Bhikkhu Anālayo, The Foundation History of the Nuns' Order (2016) — The sutta's statement on the completeness of the holy life requiring the four assemblies including nuns, and reference to the Dīrgha-āgama parallel.
- [Peoples 2013] Dion Peoples, Buddhist Critical Thinking Skills (2013) — Discussion of the context of establishing Buddhism after Mahāvīra's death and setting meaning beside meaning.
- [Pandey 1972] Lakshuman Pandey, Buddhist Conception of Omniscience (1972) — Notes the sutta's treatment of the Tathāgata's knowledge of past and future.
- [Walshe 1987] Maurice Walshe, The Long Discourses of the Buddha: A Translation of the Dīgha Nikāya (1987) — Alternative English title and discussion of relation to DN 33 and 34.
